commands.help:
Log in this home's user identity and provision the device key.

The daemon owns the login flow end to end. On a home with no account yet,
login starts the bootstrap daemon when none runs, shows the verification
URL and user code, opens the browser (not with --no-open), and waits for
that one daemon operation until it reaches serving. On a home that already
has an owner, login starts the serving daemon if needed and runs one
daemon-driven reauthentication until serving; logging in with a different
account when local business data exists is refused. A device that cannot be
registered never rolls the identity back: login still succeeds and reports
``device.ready: false`` with ``retry: serving-start``.

After a new login, confirm organization invitations one at a time on a
TTY. Non-TTY and --json runs only report pending invitations. To accept
all invitations explicitly, use org pending --accept-all.

params.help: Do not launch a browser; still print the verification URI and user code.
Seconds allowed without daemon startup phase progress when login starts the daemon for login (env: HYPRIAL_INIT_READY_TIMEOUT).

commands.help:
Remove this home's user login without removing machine or agent keys.

Logout is one daemon request: the daemon removes secrets/login.json plus
the Casdoor identity fields that login wrote in settings.json. It never
removes agent credentials, Tailcat device keys, or unrelated settings. The
command starts the daemon when none runs; a serving daemon then returns to
the no-account phase in the same process, and the command does not wait for
that. A home with no user login reports not-logged-in.

It does not revoke already-issued access tokens at the issuer.
Such tokens can remain valid until expiry.

params.help: Confirm removal of this home's user login.

commands.help:
Start the GUI and wait in the foreground.

One host process serves the GUI and the same-origin session, and with the
daemon driver it relays requests to the daemon in-process (request-http
v1), so no separate backend process is started; the explicit contract-mock
driver instead runs its own Node child.  The daemon is the only long-lived
backend and keeps running when the GUI is closed.  The installed
wheel serves its built-in verified assets; a source checkout builds the GUI
and serves ``gui/dist``, and ``--live-source`` puts the Vite development
server behind the host instead.  ``--with-dev-tools`` adds the developer
tool layer to either; ``dev`` is both flags.  The backend driver defaults
to the daemon.  Retired verbs are rejected.

commands.help: Inspect and authorize Lark App tenant scopes.
Inventory declared and tenant-authorized Lark App scopes.

Get the App's scopes authorized by the tenant.

Default: ask the tenant admin to approve the scopes the App has *already*
declared (the v6 scopes/apply endpoint). It cannot add an undeclared scope,
publish an App version, or approve the request; the returned official URL is
the manual administrator handoff. An App with nothing declared but
unapproved therefore comes back as 'nothing_to_request'.

--interactive instead runs the official device-authorization flow against
this adapter's existing App and prints a verification link. Because the
scope/event declaration rides along with that link as the 'addons'
parameter, one confirmation both declares and authorizes the scopes -- which
is the only way to reach a capability the App never declared. The link goes
to stderr, so '--json' stdout stays exactly one JSON value.

Optional capabilities are never requested implicitly: pass --capability
group-history to include im:message.group_msg, which lets the App read every
message in its groups rather than only @-mentions.

--scope is a separate, link-only handoff for already-known scope names. It
cannot be combined with --interactive or --capability and never calls a
Lark API.

commands.help: Watch the lark-cli USER credential: detect expiry, walk the device flow to 'one click away', and push the link to a human.

Check the lark-cli user identity; escalate to a one-click link.

* ready/valid -> silent ok, nobody is bothered;
* needs_refresh -> one side-effect-free read triggers lark-cli's lazy
  refresh; if that recovers the token, still silent (this is the
  unattended path and it never notifies);
* missing/dead refresh -> `lark-cli auth login --no-wait` mints a
  verification link that is pushed to --notify-route, then
  `hyprial adapter user-auth complete` finishes the flow after the human clicks.
  Re-notification is cooled down per app (default 1h) and a still-valid
  pending link is never replaced by a newer one.

params.help: Adapter route name (as in `hyprial adapter route list`) that receives the authorization link. Precedence: this flag > $HYPRIAL_LARK_REAUTH_NOTIFY_ROUTE > the route remembered from an earlier run. Without one, the link only lands in the local state file and this command's output.
Registered local identity the notification is sent from ($HYPRIAL_LARK_REAUTH_FROM is the fallback). Required for delivery.

commands.help: Read and write operator switches in settings.json.

Set an operator switch in settings.json.

``autoUpgrade`` (spec autoupdate-isolated-home r1) gates every automatic
self-upgrade: the daemon scheduler and its ``autoupdate run`` child skip
until this is explicitly ``true``.  The manual
``hyprial daemon upgrade`` is an operator's explicit act and stays ungated.

``forwarding.mode`` is the durable forwarding switch: ``auto`` (the
default) forwards through the sidecar on a sidecar-joined home, ``off``
disables it -- including any explicit or generated forwarding variables
-- and ``on`` refuses to start the daemon without it.
``HYPRIAL_FORWARDING`` in the daemon's environment still wins.  It takes
effect on the next daemon start.

``workerProxy.*`` is hyprial's own proxy for model-vendor workers:
``url`` (http/https; empty clears the whole setting and restores the
ambient behaviour), ``vendors`` (the model-vendor families that use it,
default ``openai,anthropic``; every other vendor's worker gets NO proxy
variables) and ``noProxy`` (the workers' ``NO_PROXY``; empty keeps the
daemon's own).  It is read at each worker launch, so it applies to the
next launch without a daemon restart.

params.help: Config key (supported: autoUpgrade, lsRemoteTimeoutSeconds, forwarding.mode, org.fetchSource, workerProxy.url, workerProxy.vendors, workerProxy.noProxy, dispatch.reminder, modelBinding.operationLimit).

commands.help: Create, inspect and destroy the agents registered on this machine. An agent is an identity plus its configuration; the harness it runs on is a runtime binding, not part of the agent, so the same agent can be started on claude today and pi tomorrow.

Register a new agent on this machine.

The name is the agent's identity within agent:<owner>:<machine>:, and only
one agent may hold it -- creating a second agent under a name already in
use fails, whether or not anything is currently running under it. The name
is freed only by 'hyprial agent destroy'.

Without --config, creation materializes a minimal explicit config in the
agent home so claude, codex, and pi use agent-home P2. Without --cwd, the
agent home's workspace directory is used.

A name says nothing about a harness: an agent called 'pi-ds4' is just an
agent called 'pi-ds4', and it can run on claude. To move an existing agent
to another harness, start it there; that rebinds the same agent rather
than creating a new one, so it is not a name conflict.

Credentials: a captured Claude default ('agent provider login claude
--actor OWNER --setup-token --default') grants its token to new agents with
--preferred-harness claude. A captured native default copies the named
owner's login instead. PAC and lifecycle creation use the same policy.
Legacy provider-name defaults still seed from host login in this CLI only;
re-run provider login --default --actor OWNER to bind a Claude source for PAC.

Default working directory (defaults to the agent home's workspace/).

Attach an externally supervised harness as an agent (custody=external).

Registers the agent identity, or reuses it when it is already an
external-custody agent, and makes the harness its single cell member;
the cell membership follows the agent record, so members added to it by
hand are removed.  The daemon never starts, restores or stops that
harness ('hyprial agent start' refuses an attached agent): messages to
the agent wait in its inbox and the harness reads them with the message
commands.  Without a registered session, reading with --from <name>
works only while sender authentication is in observe mode (the default);
under enforce, reply and ack use --from user:<owner> --on-behalf-of
<name> and reading has no operator form yet.  Repeating the command
changes nothing.  A name held by a daemon-managed agent is refused.

destroy, and it refuses a daemon-managed agent.

commands.help:
Record, inspect, revoke, or reason about a capability grant.

``add`` records a capability grant: see-actors and send-to are enforced on
each applicable request, while other capabilities are recorded for their
owning entry points. ``list`` reads the actor's active records (or its
append-only audit history with --audit) and ``revoke`` removes one.

``check`` evaluates a what-if capability decision from CLI arguments: it
does not read the grant ledger, and the result names the entry point that
owns the capability (AT10).

``visibility`` evaluates what-if see-actors / send-to decisions from CLI
arguments: it does not read the grant ledger (AT09 decision core).

Permanently delete an agent. THIS CANNOT BE UNDONE.

Destroying an agent stops its connectors, deletes its record, and discards
its undelivered messages. There is no tombstone and no revival: messages
already sent to this agent lose a resolvable recipient, and recreating the
same name later gives you a new, empty agent -- not this one back.
Interactive terminals may confirm after seeing the workspace inventory;
non-interactive callers must pass --yes.

params.help: Actor name of the agent to destroy.

commands.help:
Show scoped cell run state, plus legacy turn and queue diagnostics.

RUN STATE comes only from the daemon's shared runState projection, not
logs or process sampling. Missing runState is unsupported/unknown.
The reason, measured turn age, scope, certainty and permission capability
remain explicit; suspected-stuck is not proof of deadlock or a kill policy.
LEGACY is the prior log/contact heuristic (JSON state/stateDetail), not
a current run-state claim. Presence, queue and permission coverage differ.

Headless legacy turn fields come from the current worker-generation JSONL log and
stay null when that generation boundary cannot be proven.
Interactive Claude ``turnCount`` and ``lastTurnEndedAtMs`` come from fenced

marks when that partial count began. The end timestamp is daemon receipt

commands.help: Manage your own model-vendor API keys, sealed to your devices.
List your stored keys and the agents granted each; never any key value.

params.help: Only keys of this model vendor.

commands.help:
Delete a key and revoke every agent grant that uses it.

Without --yes the affected agents are listed on stderr and you are asked to
confirm; non-interactive and --json callers must pass --yes.

params.help: Skip the confirmation listing affected agents.

commands.help:
Store a new API key for a model vendor, sealed to this device.

The key is read only from stdin (--api-key-stdin) and never printed. Every
call creates a new key; agents use it only after 'hyprial agent provider allow'.

params.help: Model vendor name, e.g. openai or deepseek.
Read the API key as one line from non-TTY stdin (required).
Optional display label for this key.
Environment variable name the key is injected as; repeatable.

commands.help:
Rotate a key's data-encryption key and reissue its agent grants.

With --replace-stdin the API key itself is replaced too; the new value is
read only from stdin and never printed.

params.help: Also replace the API key with one line read from non-TTY stdin.
